extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor organizations, occupational health researchers, and public commenters on OSHA's proposed heat standard
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory risk-assessment and evidentiary rationale used to set heat-exposure triggers and estimate incidence of occupational heat-related injuries, illnesses, and fatalities for OSHA's proposed standard. Includes data-source methods, limitations, and evidence-evaluation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of heat-related fatalities using OIICS codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat-related fatalities can be identified with an event code (“Exposure to environmental heat”) and/or a nature code (“Effects of heat and light”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use OIICS event/exposure and nature codes to classify fatalities in BLS CFOI; exclude secondary heat sources (e.g., ovens) when identifying ambient heat fatalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of BLS CFOI counts with CPS denominators for fatality rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate fatality rates using BLS CFOI counts for heat-related deaths and worker population estimates from CPS to derive rates (per 100,000 workers or per FTE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA used BLS fatality counts (e.g., 2011-2022) and CPS employment and average hours worked to estimate total FTEs and average annual fatality rates; note limitations discussed elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sector- and occupation-stratified incidence estimates over whole-workforce denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: Stratified estimates (by sector, industry, or occupation) provide more accurate estimates of incidence among workers actually exposed to heat, because whole-workforce denominators include many unexposed workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: agriculture and construction show substantially higher rates than overall workforce (e.g., 0.306 vs 0.022 fatalities/100,000 in Gubernot et al.). Use stratified denominators to better reflect true risk to exposed workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denominator selection should reflect exposed worker-time and hot-season exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the total worker population and full-year worker-time dilutes incidence estimates; denominators should better reflect the population/time actually exposed to hazardous heat (e.g., seasonal/month-limited exposures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting to hotter months (e.g., Q3) or to workers whose jobs involve heat exposure yields higher and more relevant rates; OSHA notes risk would be higher when considering exposed worker-days only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for undercounting in surveillance data (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing surveillance data (SOII, workers' compensation, hospital data, CFOI) substantially undercount heat-related injuries, illnesses, and fatalities; reported incidence estimates likely are vast underestimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple data streams, consider linkage studies, and interpret surveillance-based incidence as conservative lower bounds on true incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of BLS SOII for estimating heat-related incidence
rubrics_metrics.description: BLS SOII focuses on OSHA-recordable cases and those involving days away from work, which inherently limits its ability to estimate all occupational injuries and illnesses and leads to underestimation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SOII may miss up to ~58% of OSHA-recordable HRIs (cases not involving days away). Linkage studies and comparisons to state systems/compensation databases show SOII can miss substantial numbers of cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of employer underreporting on OSHA logs
rubrics_metrics.description: Employer under-recording/unrecording arises from worker non-reporting (fear, retaliation), use of on-site medical units (that mask reportable care), misunderstanding of reporting requirements, and disincentives tied to premiums/contracting/inspections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA NEP inspections found ~47% of establishments had unrecorded/under-recorded cases; studies found many employers not maintaining logs or failing aspects of recordkeeping compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workers' compensation data limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Workers' compensation data may capture cases not in SOII but are not nationally uniform (state differences, multiple insurers) and can miss cases due to eligibility rules or underutilization by workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workers may avoid filing claims for reasons including fear, lack of knowledge, perceived effort, or considering the injury part of the job; percent captured varies substantially by state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospital discharge data limitations for work-relatedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Hospital discharge data do not include work-relatedness as an inclusion criterion; researchers must infer or identify work-related cases (e.g., workers' comp as payer or external cause codes), which can undercount work-related HRIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External cause codes and payer fields are imperfect (often missing/inaccurate). Researchers should take additional steps to assess work-relatedness and may miss cases when those indicators are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and variability of ICD coding for heat-related cases
rubrics_metrics.description: ICD codes are billing-oriented and provider-dependent; providers may not recognize or record heat as a cause (e.g., syncope coded as R55 instead of T67.1), leading to underreporting in code-based surveillance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should use all possible fields (primary diagnosis, secondary diagnosis, underlying cause, contributing cause) and unstructured fields (chief complaint) to identify cases; adoption of ICD-10 increased capture in some systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: CFOI strengths and classification limitations for fatalities
rubrics_metrics.description: CFOI is the most complete authoritative source for fatal workplace injuries, but classification relies on death certificates, OSHA reports, news, coroner reports, and may misclassify heat-related deaths; criteria vary by state and certifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that heat as a contributing factor may be missed when other causes (e.g., cardiac arrest) are recorded; alternative epidemiological methods (e.g., temperature-attributable mortality) can yield higher counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use WBGT-based triggers anchored to NIOSH REL and RAL
rubrics_metrics.description: WBGT triggers in the proposed standard are based on NIOSH exposure limits (REL and RAL), which have empirical support and are sensitive in capturing unsustainable heat exposures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When available, WBGT-based limits provide experimental physiology-based benchmarks that inform protective action levels, especially in high radiant heat conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of heat index-based triggers (initial and high triggers)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA preliminarily selected an initial heat trigger of 80 °F (heat index) and a high heat trigger of 90 °F (heat index) based on a combination of observational and experimental evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational evidence showed the vast majority of known occupational heat-related fatalities and nonfatal HRIs occur above the 80 °F trigger; WBGT/experimental evidence suggests 90 °F is an appropriate level for additional controls when radiant heat is high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criterion: prioritize sensitivity for screening triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriateness of a heat-index screening level is evaluated by its sensitivity—the degree to which a particular heat index value can be used to screen for potential risk of HRIs and fatalities (capture the majority of cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA sought a highly sensitive screening level so that most fatal and nonfatal HRIs would occur above the trigger; sensitivity tradeoffs discussed (e.g., 80 °F captures ~96% of historic fatalities in one study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider multifactorial contributors to individual HRI risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk of HRI is influenced by workload, PPE, acclimatization status, ability to self-pace, prior-day exposures, medications, and comorbidities, and these should be considered when interpreting exposure-trigger evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational studies didn't account for these modifiers individually; OSHA treats retrospective observational data as valuable because cases include populations where these factors vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoffs between experimental and observational evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental physiology studies offer controlled exposure measurements but may not mimic real-world multi-day exposures or diverse worker populations; observational studies reflect real-world exposures but may suffer exposure misclassification (e.g., using weather-station maxima).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA used both streams to inform triggers—using experimental WBGT guidance and observational heat-index associations to balance internal validity and external applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for matching weather data to HRI/fatality events
rubrics_metrics.description: Recreate heat index for event days using weather monitor-based temperature and dew point measurements (daily maximum temperature and daily average dew point); if no monitor in the county, use the next closest monitor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach underlies several observational studies (e.g., Gubernot) and introduces possible exposure misclassification if spatial mismatch exists between monitor and event location.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Weather Service excessive heat event (EHE) criteria (for comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: NWS EHE directive: issue excessive heat warnings when there will be 2 or more days that meet or exceed a heat index of 105 °F for the Northern U.S. and 110 °F for the Southern U.S., with temperatures not falling below 75 °F (local offices may vary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by researchers as a comparator; OSHA evaluated whether fatalities occurred on days meeting these EHE thresholds and noted Gubernot's simpler criterion for EHE sensitivity assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute denominators using FTEs (total workers × average hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: For some rate calculations OSHA used total number of workers and average hours worked to estimate total FTEs per year for denominator in fatality/illness rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method aims to account for part-time/variable-hours work but still may include unexposed worker-time unless restricted to exposed worker populations or seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use linkage and multi-source comparisons to assess underreporting magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Link SOII to workers' compensation and other state/local surveillance systems to estimate undercount; studies found SOII missed substantial proportions of cases (e.g., state-based systems had 5–10× more cases for some conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA cites linkage studies (e.g., Rosenman, Wuellner) and recommends considering such evidence when evaluating surveillance completeness for HRIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to estimate rates restricted to exposed populations or hot-season periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimating rates limited to sector/occupation groups or restricted to months with heat exposure (e.g., July–September) yields several-fold higher rates than annual averages across all workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies restricting denominator to third quarter found much higher incidence, supporting the claim that annual whole-population rates understate risk for exposed workers.
